items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-05-11
items.q: I just want to say that, that Louis Armstrong is the only one that happened to mention in his biography of George Moret.

ctx.x: I know Natty said he was raised that way.

On French, that's right. And I still talk French now. And then when someone, when I can talk with someone. So the first lesson I had at Nelson Jean's house, he was a great friend of the family, but he liked to take a drink of wine. So I went on my first lesson. And then, while he told me to get, had an old cornet that I bought somewhere. I don't know where it was. And anyhow, my daddy found it for me, I believe. And I was too young to remember. He wanted me to learn how to clean the horn. So I decided to clean…
We talked to one of the brothers of the old men. There was an old Lorenzo and a Louis Teo, Papa Teo.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-05-27
items.q: Well then you come along with Louis, and now you have a different vein all together.

ctx.x: Like you go over there and you hear Buddy. Is there anybody on the record that sounds like Buddy that you've ever heard?

Not that I can recall right now. But I tell you what. Punch Miller, when Punch was young, he copied Buddy B.T. style as close as he could. But today, no I can't say that I, well, if you listen to my records, you'll hear a trumpet player named Billy Douglas. I think Billy Douglas is one of the greatest trumpet players I've ever heard in my life. Technical. The tonation wasn't the best in the world, but as a technical trumpet player, making things that we musicians hear are almost impossible, you get a vivid idea…
Do you think the musicians are a hack of the play of that kind of music?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: And when I first had Louis as my guest in 1931 in Oklahoma City, I wired him and I told him that I'd have his favorite dish when he got there.

ctx.x: Served beans? Red beans and rice. And donuts, yeah.

That's a traditional food for, well, here's what they do. They cook this food the day before. And the early morning, everybody would get ready to go on the street. And then you come to the house, you get your dinner or you go to a friend's house. And usually you had your donuts and your beans and rice and pickled meat, whatever they call it. Yeah. That was one of Louis's great dishes. And when I first had Louis as my guest in 1931 in Oklahoma City, I wired him and I told him that I'd have his favorite dish when…
Yeah, well, I get red bean hungry sometimes. I do too.
